items.content:
Global waterways have become critical pressure points in global supply chains.

The Panama Canal and Suez Canal were once viewed mainly as ocean freight infrastructure.

Today, they influence boardroom conversations around inventory, sourcing strategy, lead times, and working capital.

Panama Canal
→ Critical for Asia - US East Coast trade
→ Recently impacted by drought conditions and water shortages
→ Vessel draft restrictions reduced throughput and created congestion risk

Suez Canal
→ Critical for Asia - Europe trade
→ Facing ongoing Red Sea security risks
→ Carriers rerouting around the Cape of Good Hope added time and cost back into global networks

Both waterways shorten shipping routes by thousands of miles.
Both move tens of millions of containers every year.
And both have exposed how dependent global supply chains still are on a handful of critical trade corridors.

For logistics leaders, this is no longer just an ocean carrier issue.
It impacts:
→ Freight costs
→ Inventory positioning
→ Transit reliability
→ Cash flow

The companies navigating this environment best are modeling alternatives before disruption forces the decision.

➜ Which disruption would create the bigger operational impact for your network?

items.content:
Some operations break from too much friction. 
Others break from too much variation.

Treating them the same creates expensive mistakes.

Lean optimizes flow
- Eliminates waste so work flows faster.
- Best when processes are heavy, slow, or over-engineered.
Lean asks: Why does this step exist?

Six Sigma optimizes reliability
- Reduces variation so outcomes are reliable.
- Best when defects, rework, or quality misses are the problem.
Six Sigma asks: Why does this step fail sometimes?

The relationship
Lean accelerates.
Six Sigma stabilizes.

Speed without stability creates chaos.
Stability without speed creates drag.

Bottom line
If the system is slow → start with Lean
If results are inconsistent → start with Six Sigma

Strong operators focus less on methodology and more on what is actually breaking the system.

➜ What breaks first in your operation: friction or variation?

items.content:
Tariff Update | New 85% Rule Creates Winners & Losers in Manufacturing

President Trump signed a proclamation updating Section 232 tariffs on certain steel, aluminum, and copper products. The changes take effect June 8, 2026, and remain in place through December 31, 2027.

Key Changes

1. Agricultural Equipment Tariffs Reduced
Certain agricultural equipment, including combines and harvesters, will move from a 25% tariff to a reduced 15% tariff rate.

2. More Industrial Equipment Added to 15% Category
The temporary 15% tariff category is expanded to include:
- Mobile industrial equipment
- Forklifts
- Bulldozers
- Certain residential HVAC systems and components

This lowers duties compared to the standard derivative product tariff rates.

3. Incentive to Use US Metals
Products containing at least 85% US melted and poured steel or 85% US smelted and cast aluminum or copper can qualify for a lower effective tariff rate of 10%.

The previous threshold was 95%, making qualification easier.

4. New Products Added to Coverage
Additional derivative products now subject to Section 232 duties include:
- Aluminum lithographic plates
- Steel racks

The administration stated this is intended to prevent tariff circumvention.

5. Special Treatment for Trade Partners
Certain products from EU, UK, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, Switzerland, Liechtenstein, Argentina, Ecuador, El Salvador, & Guatemala will generally face a total tariff burden of 15% rather than higher Section 232 rates.

6. USMCA Content Benefit
Products imported from Canada & Mexico may pay tariffs only on the non-US portion of the product, with a minimum tariff rate of 15%.

Who wins?
→ Suppliers with 85%+ US metal content
→ USMCA supply chains

Who loses?
→ Import-heavy sourcing models
→ Low traceability supply chains

Bottom line: Can your suppliers qualify for the lower tariff rates?

items.content:
FTZs and bonded warehouses both defer duties.
Only one can eliminate them.

They’re often treated as interchangeable.
They’re not.
The difference shows up in cost, flexibility, and risk.

→ Foreign Trade Zone (FTZ)
Best when goods are changed...manufactured, assembled, repaired, or re-exported.
Duties are triggered only if products enter US commerce.

→ Bonded Warehouse
Best when goods are paused...stored short-to-medium term before entering the US market.
Duties are deferred, not avoided.

Where teams get this wrong
- Using bonded warehouses expecting FTZ-level savings
- Paying duty on damaged or scrapped goods unnecessarily
- Missing inverted tariff opportunities
- Optimizing finance without aligning operations & compliance

Bottom line
If your operation adds value or complexity → look hard at an FTZ.
If you just need time and flexibility before US entry → a bonded warehouse may be enough.

Same imports.
Very different outcomes.

➜ Which one has created more surprises for your team: FTZs or bonded warehouses?

Trade Update | US & China Summit Highlights

The White House released a fact sheet following President Trump’s visit to China outlining several new agreements and areas of cooperation between the US and China.

Operators were hoping for tariff relief from the US & China summit.
It didn’t happen.

Now supply chain teams are asking: Was this a stabilization meeting… or the first step toward future tariff negotiations?”

Here’s the breakdown:

→ The US and China agreed to establish two new government-led institutions:
 • US-China Board of Trade
 • US-China Board of Investment

These groups are intended to manage trade and investment discussions across non-sensitive sectors.

→ China agreed to address US concerns around rare earth and critical mineral supply chains

This includes materials like neodymium, scandium, yttrium, and indium that are important for manufacturing, aerospace, semiconductors, batteries, and defense-related industries.

→ China approved an initial purchase of 200 Boeing aircraft
This is China’s first Boeing purchase commitment since 2017 and represents a major win for US aerospace manufacturing.

→ China committed to purchase at least $17B annually in US agricultural products through 2028
Separate soybean purchase commitments from 2025 remain in place.

→ China restored market access for US beef facilities
More than 400 US beef facilities had expired approvals renewed, with additional work planned to remove remaining suspensions.

→ China resumed poultry imports from certain US states
Imports will resume from states cleared by USDA for avian influenza concerns.

What was notably absent:
→ No announced Section 301 tariff rollback
→ No broad tariff normalization framework
→ No major structural trade agreement tied to tariff reductions

Bottom line: The summit focused more on stabilizing the relationship, securing strategic supply chain commitments, and reopening targeted trade flows than on removing tariffs. 

For supply chain leaders, the biggest near-term impacts may come from rare earth access and agricultural market reopening.

But the larger tariff question still remains unanswered.

With President Xi expected to visit the US this fall, many companies will now be watching to see whether this summit was simply a stabilization meeting… or the foundation for a future tariff negotiation round.

Many teams treat forecasting and planning as the same thing.

When the forecast shifts but the plan doesn’t, the result is predictable:
- Inventory building in the wrong nodes
- Expedites and short production runs
- Working capital creep
- Service levels slipping

Better forecasts help.
But stronger planning processes are what actually protect profitability.

items.content:
Two of the most expensive words in ocean shipping:
Demurrage and Detention.

Most teams know they’re expensive.
Far fewer understand the difference.

Both charges occur when containers exceed the carrier’s free time...typically 3-7 days depending on the port and carrier.

Here’s the difference operators need to know:

➝ Demurrage
Container stuck inside the port
- Clock starts when the container is discharged from the vessel
- Applies while the container remains in the terminal
- Common causes: customs delays, paperwork issues, or no truck arranged

➝ Detention
Container stuck outside the port
- Clock starts when the container gates out
- Applies while the container is being unloaded or awaiting return
- Common causes: slow unloading or delayed empty return

A simple way to remember it:
Demurrage = Port storage problem
Detention = Equipment return problem

Both exist for one reason: Carriers need containers moving, not sitting.

Ocean shipping doesn’t end when the vessel arrives.
For many teams, that’s when the cost clock actually begins.

➜ Supply Chain VPs: how is your team tracking demurrage and detention risk before charges hit?

items.content:
There's a version of me that became a reindeer farmer as nature intended (growing up in arctic Lapland it wasn’t exactly an eccentric career option.) 

Instead, I became a CEO, which, according to this graph, is a career I mostly spend in restaurants, airports, and all the spaces between them. 

Evidence from week 2 of a 3 week travel:
- 2 intercontinental flights
- 3 cities
- 9 business lunches and dinners
- 33 meetings 

Early on in your career, you point to something at the end of the day and say, 'Cool, I built that.'
 
Stay at it long enough, and your calendar looks nothing like the work you knew before and a lot like…wining and dining. Gone is the satisfaction of concrete achievements!

To my colleagues, having dinner looks suspiciously like not working, but sit across enough tables in Copenhagen, Chicago, and London, and something starts happening…

You hear how the same problem takes a different form in every city. You get to test whether your assumptions hold up to reality (some don't and that's exactly why you must test them)... All that perspective builds so slowly that, for a long time, it doesn't feel like it's building at all. 

Do it anyway. One day, it clicks, and you realize those conversations have been raw material for every half-decent decision you've made.
 
So yes, nice dinners are involved. But by then, you know exactly what they're for. I can tell you it's not the menu.

Big thanks to everyone who shared a meal with me these past few weeks!

items.content:
In a market where everyone can demo anything, what do you actually bet on?

A year ago, building a convincing procurement AI prototype took a team, now it takes an afternoon. Great news for innovation and a real problem for CPOs trying to make technology decisions.

My advice to CPOs is simple: stay anchored to the problems, not the tools. Double down on your data foundation. 

I mean all of it, not just the structured spend data you've been building for years, but the unstructured data too. Every email with a supplier, every negotiation on Teams, every contract discussion that never made it into your ERP.

Data is the one investment that holds its value regardless of which AI tools win in the long run. For everything else, run pilots, stay curious, and experience the technology yourself concretely. The tools change every week, the problems don't.

If getting your existing data foundation AI-ready is on your agenda, we have a webinar on exactly that next week. Bain and Hershey's joining us. Link in comments.

items.content:
There are two kinds of people in procurement right now. Those using Claude every day. And those who will be in a few months.
Both groups are about to have a very interesting year.

I've gone a bit deep on agents lately. What's already possible for procurement specifically is, well, a lot.

And here's what becomes clear pretty fast: when any team can spin up an AI agent in a week, the race is no longer about who has the best AI. It's about who has the best data to back it up and that is a fundamentally different game. Most procurement functions haven’t fully reckoned with what a dealbreaker that will be.

Procurement teams are at wildly different stages in this new wave of AI disruption, but the direction is clear enough that waiting for certainty, in itself, is a decision.

We've been figuring out what this means for procurement. The tooling, the data, the next steps. SVP Product Heta Pirttijärvi and I are sharing our take in a live webinar on April 8th. 

We'll make the 45 minutes count, link in comments.
